I'm 40 years old, and I've been farming our land in Quzhou County since I finished middle school over twenty years ago. My husband works off-farm in the county town, so I make most of the day-to-day decisions on our 7 mu of flat, irrigated land on the North China Plain.

This year, I'll keep doing what has worked for us: I'll grow winter wheat and summer maize in rotation on 5 mu, and I'll plant cotton on the remaining 2 mu. The wheat-maize rotation is the safest bet here — the grain station always buys wheat, and maize prices have been steady. I sowed the wheat last October after the National Day holiday; it is in the field now and I am managing it through to harvest in early June. Right after we harvest the wheat, I'll direct-seed summer maize into the stubble without tilling — there's no time to waste between crops. For wheat, I use improved seeds, usually Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502 from the local supply shop. For maize, I only plant hybrid seeds; Denghai 605 is what my neighbors and I have been using because it yields well and resists lodging. 

The 2 mu of cotton is for cash income. Cotton is more work — especially the spraying and hand-picking — but with just 2 mu I can manage it myself and the returns are better than grain. I will rotary till the cotton plot in April and sow soon after.

For management: I rotary till before wheat sowing, but I do not till for maize. I apply about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as a base dressing for all three crops. For wheat, I also topdress about 100 jin of urea in spring with the green-up irrigation. I irrigate wheat four times, maize two or three times depending on rainfall, and cotton three times. Pests are a constant problem, so I spray wheat about four times total, maize three times, and cotton ten times because the bollworms are relentless here. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 1000 jin per mu of wheat, 1150 jin per mu of maize, and 500 jin per mu of cotton.
